items.record: The case is a criminal one. A man was convicted of rape on eyewitness identification and later exonerated: "Mr. Cotton was convicted by a jury of one count of rape and one count of burglary."
items.reading: The reading guesses an administrative or regulatory matter such as welfare determinations, a safety failure, or automated harm.
items.loss: This is the basic domain and the kind of harm involved.

items.record: The text is a narrative case summary written after exoneration, not an institution issuing guidance: "The results indicated that Mr. Cotton was not the source of the DNA."
items.reading: The reading calls it an official state document that gives procedural guidance and directs affected people into channels.
items.loss: This is the genre and purpose of the document.

items.record: The central harm is one wrongly convicted individual and one misled victim, not a dispersed mass of isolated claimants: "Mr. Cotton was released after spending more than 10 years in prison."
items.reading: The reading describes many isolated individuals who cannot see that their case is one of many.
items.loss: This is who the affected parties are and how many there are.

items.record: The error came from a sincere but mistaken eyewitness who hesitated at first: "it is between number four and number five". She settled on a choice after a second viewing and voice repetition.
items.reading: The reading treats the illusion as bureaucratic framing that the institution produces.
items.loss: This is the actual mechanism of error, which was fallible human memory reinforced by procedure.

items.record: Repeated identification hardened the witness's certainty. She went from photo array to live lineup to courtroom testimony: "She again identified Mr. Cotton as her attacker."
items.loss: This is the sequence by which a tentative belief became fixed testimony.

items.record: The second victim first could not identify anyone. At retrial she named Cotton: "saying she had been too afraid to identify him right after the crime."
items.loss: This shows how witness accounts shifted over time to fit the prosecution.

items.record: The courts swung back and forth. A conviction was reversed because exculpatory evidence had been excluded: "the defense should have been allowed to present the evidence of the other victim's identification of someone else". A retrial followed with more charges, and the conviction was affirmed.
items.reading: The reading says conflict was absorbed into procedure, with the record holding until a later rupture.
items.loss: This is the actual back-and-forth sequence of appeal, reversal, and retrial.

items.record: The real perpetrator was put in front of the victims and both rejected him, which blocked the alternate-suspect defense: "Ms. Thompson-Cannino and the other woman both contended that he was not their attacker."
items.loss: This is the moment where the true culprit was directly visible and still excluded.

items.record: Circumstantial physical evidence, a foam insole and a flashlight, corroborated a wrong identification. The alibi came only from relatives.
items.loss: This is how weak evidence was stacked to support the conviction.

items.record: Resolution came through scientific testing that the defense requested, plus a database match and a confession: "confirmed a match with Bobbie Poole... he had admitted to other inmates."
items.reading: The reading expects rupture through aggregation of cases, journalism, litigation, or an inquiry.
items.loss: This is the specific trigger and mechanism of the reversal.

items.record: The resolution was clean and cooperative. Prosecution and defense jointly moved to dismiss, the real offender pleaded guilty, and the governor pardoned Cotton: "The district attorney and the defense filed a motion to dismiss all charges."
items.reading: The reading describes an entangled conflict with institutional rationalizing and possible burial.
items.loss: This is the actual outcome and the institution's response.

items.record: The wrongly convicted man and the victim who misidentified him reconciled and became partners in advocacy: "They became good friends and began to travel around the country to speak about wrongful convictions."
items.loss: This is the relationship between the two central parties after the case.

items.record: The case was turned into a push for reform of eyewitness identification procedures, and the two co-wrote a memoir.
items.loss: This is the case's downstream reform role and its public afterlife.

items.record: The man rebuilt his life after release, including work at the lab that cleared him and a modest state payment: "got a job in the warehouse of LabCorp, the company that tested the DNA evidence."
items.loss: This is the personal aftermath and the remedy he received.

items.record: A serial pattern of linked attacks with a shared method was known at trial: "entered the house's back door after smashing a porch light."
items.loss: This is the factual crime pattern that linked the cases.
